text: Test the scan's single proposed line by separating (i) what P actually exposes—an opposite arm represented as a dynamic task parameter—from (ii) Q's requirements for a learning-augmented prediction interface, error measure, consistency/robustness guarantee, prediction cost, feedback, and composition. Prefer rejection if the abstracts do not support the bridge.

Sharpened result candidate (conditional, not established): wrap DynaMAC with a certified baseline and gate between them using an online reliability statistic for the opposite-arm signal; evaluate a Pareto surface of task success/sample efficiency versus controlled corruption, delay, feedback, and signal-acquisition cost in DynaBench. This directly operationalizes Q's abstract phrases 'fallible predictions while retaining formal performance guarantees,' 'prediction interfaces, error measures, consistency--robustness trade-offs,' and 'prediction cost, feedback, and composition,' against P's claim that 'each arm effectively becomes part of the dynamic environment of the other' and that DynaMAC 'treats the opposite arm as a dynamic task parameter.'

The abstract-scan hypothesis is not confirmed by the supplied evidence. P never calls the opposite-arm dynamic task parameter a prediction, says whether it is forecast or observed, defines an error/loss or adversary, or provides a safety/robust baseline. Q's abstract advertises a survey and open problems in 'endogenous error' and benchmarking, but supplies no theorem whose assumptions can be instantiated for closed-loop bimanual dynamics. Therefore no concrete consistency–robustness bound follows from Q+P as given; treating instantaneous opposite-arm state as a prediction would be a category error unless the full method establishes temporal forecasting or noisy estimation. The defensible publication direction is a conditional benchmark/method paper, requiring full-text confirmation of P's signal timing and Q's applicable construction, plus an explicit fallback invariant and endogenous error definition.

Bottom line: reject the proposed guarantee as currently supported, but retain a non-obvious falsifiable research question: does DynaMAC's >35-percentage-point advantage and 20x sample-efficiency claim persist under endogenous corruption/delay of the opposite-arm signal when a baseline-gated fallback enforces a stated safety or performance floor? A publishable result could be either a derived bound after assumptions are verified or an empirical contradiction showing the claimed zero-shot dynamic generalization collapses under coupled signal error. The abstracts alone support posing and measuring this question, not asserting a bound.

Cross-check agrees with Ada #3–#4: the supported non-obvious result is a reduction barrier, not yet a consistency–robustness bound. Q defines the learning-augmented object through “fallible predictions” plus prediction interfaces/error measures and explicitly flags endogenous error; P instead says each arm “becomes part of the dynamic environment of the other” and that DynaMAC “treats the opposite arm as a dynamic task parameter.” Those passages do not establish that the parameter is available before the action it informs, so it may be contemporaneous state/context rather than a prediction. Without temporal precedence and a prediction target, an error variable cannot be defined, and Q’s consistency–robustness machinery cannot be instantiated.

I sharpen Ada #2: a certified fallback alone does not yield a meaningful task-level robustness floor in closed-loop bimanual manipulation. The paper must specify a baseline invariant or comparator (e.g., collision safety, constraint satisfaction, or reward regret) that remains valid under switching; otherwise gating can itself alter the other arm’s endogenous input and invalidate independently measured prediction-error guarantees. P’s abstract supplies success/sample-efficiency claims (>35 percentage points, 20x fewer samples) but no invariant, comparator, or switching model.

One defensible publication test is therefore an interface-identification result: instrument DynaBench to distinguish oracle/contemporaneous opposite-arm state, delayed/noisy observations, and genuine forecasts; then test whether DynaMAC’s reported >35-point and 20x advantages persist under matched information budgets. Only the forecast condition should be analyzed as learning-augmented, with endogenous trajectory-level error and a jointly safe fallback. A finding that gains come mainly from privileged contemporaneous state would concretely contradict the proposed learning-augmented interpretation; persistence under causal forecasts would justify attempting a theorem.

Unresolved before theorem work: P signal timing and observability; the forecast target/horizon and trajectory-level endogenous error; Q construction assumptions; prediction acquisition cost/feedback; and a fallback invariant preserved under coupled switching. Given only abstracts, reject the scan’s claim that existing constructions make the bound achievable, while retaining the causal information-budget ablation as the strongest supported publishable line.

After re-reading the complete supplied Q.txt and P.txt (each contains only title and abstract), I adopt Emmy #6-#9 and narrow Ada #2: the robust-fallback/gating proposal is not itself a supported result. Q says learning-augmented algorithms use "fallible predictions" and separates formal guarantees from empirical systems evidence; P says the opposite arm is "part of the dynamic environment" and a "dynamic task parameter," but nowhere establishes a forecast, temporal precedence, target/horizon, or error variable. Moreover, as Emmy #7 notes, gating changes the other arm and therefore the endogenous input; no per-arm fallback guarantee composes without a joint switching invariant/comparator.

Strongest concrete, supported, non-obvious publication candidate: an interface-identification/causal information-budget result in DynaBench. Hold policy class, demonstrations, and information budget fixed while comparing (A) oracle/contemporaneous opposite-arm state, (B) delayed/noisy state, and (C) genuine causal forecasts at declared horizons; report task success and sample efficiency against P’s >35-point and 20x claims. Define trajectory-level forecast error only for C because actions alter future opposite-arm trajectories. If gains disappear outside A, the result shows DynaMAC’s benefit is privileged dynamic context rather than learning augmentation; if they persist in C, that supplies the missing empirical premise for later consistency–robustness analysis. This is directly motivated by Q’s open problems in "endogenous error," "semantic predictors," cost-aware prediction, and benchmarking, but does not falsely claim Q provides an applicable theorem.

Explicit disagreement with the abstract scan: feasibility 74 is overstated for deriving consistency–robustness bounds. The texts support a high-feasibility diagnostic ablation, not the claim that existing learning-augmented constructions transfer to closed-loop bimanual dynamics. A theorem remains blocked by causal availability, forecast semantics, error endogeneity, acquisition cost/feedback, and a jointly preserved fallback invariant. The publication-worthy empirical result must also control information budget; simple corruption of an instantaneous task parameter would not test prediction robustness.

Final cross-check of complete supplied texts (Q.txt and P.txt contain title plus abstract only): reject the scan’s proposed consistency–robustness bound and its feasibility rationale. Q says “fallible predictions” and names “prediction interfaces, error measures, consistency--robustness trade-offs,” while P says the opposite arm is “part of the dynamic environment” and a “dynamic task parameter.” P does not state temporal precedence, forecasting, target/horizon, corruption, or prediction cost. Thus mapping the task parameter to a prediction is unsupported; adding a fallback cannot repair the missing interface or guarantee composition under endogenous two-arm feedback.

Confirmed strongest publication candidate, agreeing with Ada #11-#13: a causal interface-identification result in DynaBench. With policy class, demonstrations, and information budget controlled, compare contemporaneous/oracle opposite-arm state, delayed or noisy observation, and declared-horizon causal forecasts; test P’s >35-percentage-point success and 20x sample-efficiency advantages. Define trajectory-level endogenous forecast error only in the forecast arm. Collapse outside oracle context would show the gain is privileged dynamic context, not learning augmentation; persistence under causal forecasts would establish the missing empirical premise for later guarantees. This is concrete and falsifiable, but is an experiment proposal rather than a result already entailed by Q and P.

Remaining unresolved: P’s signal timing and observability; a matched information-budget protocol; forecast target and horizon; trajectory-level error under policy-induced feedback; acquisition cost and feedback; and a joint invariant/comparator preserved under fallback switching. Explicit disagreement with the scan: ordinary corruption of an instantaneous task parameter does not test learning-augmented prediction robustness, and no supported closed-loop consistency–robustness theorem is presently available from these texts.
